newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban militia close in on ousted Masood.
newsitem.headline: Taleban militia close in on ousted Masood.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia launched a two-pronged advance overnight and bottled up former defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood in his Panjsher valley stronghold, Taleban fighters said on Monday.
The militia, which captured Kabul last week, thrust forward from Charikar, 60 kms (40 miles) north of Kabul, after capturing the town in brief fighting late on Sunday, fighters said.

They said they took Jabal os-Siraj, a town just outside the Panjsher valley, after an even briefer fight, then pushed on to seize the village of Golbahar at the mouth of the narrow gorge that leads into Masood's stronghold.

Mainly ethnic Pashtun fighters said they were awaiting orders from the Taleban supreme council in Kandahar on whether to assault the valley, but that they expected to be sent into action on Monday night.
In Kabul, Taleban commander Mohammad Gul told Reuters the militia would attack the Panjsher valley, one of the few areas still under the control of the government which the Taleban ousted last week.
The fighters in Golbahar said the second prong of the overnight advance pushed north from Jabal os-Siraj, up the Salang highway that runs north from Kabul into central Asia.
They said Taleban troops had reached the southern end of a major tunnel on the highway, but aid workers in the area said they understood that Masood's troops were still in place there.
They also said that northern Uzbek militia leader Abdul Rashid Dostum had moved significant forces into the area north of the tunnel over the past few days.

In Kabul, Mohammad Gul said that there was no immediate plan to attack Dostum, a former Masood ally who split from the ousted government in 1994 and who has kept his large fighting force and small air force neutral in subsequent fighting.
"After we have captured all the ex-government areas we will negotiate with Dostum," Gul said.

It was not immediately clear how easy it would be for the Taleban, which has captured about three-quarters of Afghanistan since its birth in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago, to capture the Panjsher valley.
Masood's men held it throughout the 1980s against several major assaults by Soviet troops backing Kabul's then-communist government.
The speed of his retreat -- from Kabul to the Panjsher valley in just three days -- seems to have dismayed the ethnic Tajik people he leads.

"We just don't know what's happening. We don't know whether Masood has a plan or is just running," said one Tajik shopkeeper in Golbahar as a jeepload of Taleban fighters swept past in a cloud of dust.
He and other Tajiks said Masood's men blew up the side of the gorge leading into the valley as they retreated to form a barrier across the road.
The speed of Masood's retreat was evident all the way from Kabul, with abandoned tanks and other military vehicles along the route.
Just north of Charikar, some 30 tanks and armoured personnel carriers stood in what had been a major Masood base.
Between Jabal os-Siraj and Golbahar another couple of dozen tanks had been abandoned.
